title: The toy store lost to stores that were not toy stores
lede: Toys “R” Us outlasted every other toy chain. It was beaten by [retailers](/category/retail/) for whom toys were one aisle, priced to bring shoppers in for everything else.

blocks.title: Share of U.S. toy sales, holiday 2003
blocks.subtitle: Analyst estimates reported by the Associated Press. Kmart and KB Toys were each put at 4% to 5%; the midpoint is drawn.
blocks.source: Estimates by Sean McGowan of Harris Nesbitt Gerard, in an AP report of November 30, 2003[^34]. Estimates, not measured figures.

blocks.title: Twenty-five years of market share
blocks.subtitle: Toys “R” Us and Walmart, share of U.S. retail toy sales, at the dates we could source.
blocks.source: 1978–1997 from a reference history[^31]; 2003 is an analyst estimate[^34]. The points are unevenly spaced in time and come from different sources, so read the direction, not the slope.

blocks.title: Who won, who died
blocks.subtitle: The toy chains are gone or reduced to names. The general merchants and the website remain.

items.name: Toys “R” Us
items.text: U.S. stores liquidated in 2018.[^14][^16] The name is licensed by WHP Global.[^23]

items.name: Walmart
items.text: Estimated share of U.S. toy sales in 2003, up from 9.5% in 1990. The largest toy seller by 1999.[^31][^34]

items.name: Target
items.text: Estimated share in 2003.[^34] It later ran the relaunched toysrus.com for Tru Kids.[^21]

items.name: Amazon
items.text: What it paid in 2009 to settle with the partner whose online toy store it ran from 2000 to 2006.[^7][^32]

items.name: KB Toys
items.text: Estimated share in 2003.[^34] Toys “R” Us bought [its brand and trademarks](/kb-toys/) on September 3, 2009.[^7]

items.name: FAO Schwarz
items.text: [Acquired by Toys “R” Us in May 2009](/fao-schwarz/) and sold to ThreeSixty Group in October 2016.[^7][^37]

items.name: Child World and Lionel
items.text: The two nearest [toy superstore rivals](/child-world/) in the late 1980s, per a reference history.[^31] Neither survives; we did not source their closing dates.

blocks.source: 10-K for fiscal 2009[^7], reference history[^31], AP[^34] and press as cited. The headline figures are not like for like.

blocks.text: Currently, the leading discounters are estimated to account for approximately 45% of total sales in the United States toy market, and as their share continues to increase, we are likely to experience ongoing pricing pressures.
blocks.who: Toys “R” Us, Form 10-K for fiscal 2004, filed April 2005[^5]
